pages.title_es: Teoría de juegos 1: Lee la tabla
concepts_covered: NC1 Strategic (normal form) game: players, strategies, payoffs, bimatrix
NC2 Strict and weak dominance, dominant strategy equilibrium, dominance by a mixture (LP)
NC3 Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (with the weak dominance order caveat and the p-beauty contest)
NC4 Best response and best response to a belief (upper envelope)
NC5 Pure strategy Nash equilibrium (deviation arrows, random games, Cournot as a potential game)
NC6 Prisoner's dilemma (Axelrod numbers and the dilemma hidden in Price Wars)
NC7 Pure coordination games and focal points (pure equilibria and Pareto ranking; tipping share on page 2)
NC8, NC9, NC10 Battle of the sexes, stag hunt, chicken: pure equilibria and the symmetric 2x2 family (their mixed equilibria are on page 2)
NC19 Pareto efficiency versus equilibrium, tragedy of the commons, Pigouvian fee
NC20 Price of anarchy with Pigou's two roads (Braess only if the Braess page is not built)
pages.pitch_es: Guerra de precios se convierte en una tabla: cada planta escoge 30, 40 o 60 kt y cada celda calcula en vivo las dos utilidades con la fórmula de Cournot. Tachas las producciones que nunca convienen, ronda tras ronda, hasta quedar en (40, 40), el equilibrio de Nash, y descubres que la celda (30, 30) les daría más a las dos: un dilema del prisionero escondido en el mercado del cemento. Luego cargas los clásicos (dilema del prisionero, caza del ciervo, gallina, batalla de los sexos) o un juego al azar, y mides cuánto cuesta que cada uno juegue por su lado con n pescadores en una ciénaga y con dos vías, una de ellas congestionada.
pages.sections: File site/lab/read-the-table.html, bundle lab/lab-gtb-table (prefix gtt), eyebrow 'Lab · Proposal · Simulation'. (0) Lede plus a short 'What a game is' box: players, strategies, payoffs that depend on everyone's choices; rationality and common knowledge stated once; ordinal payoffs suffice here, page 2 needs cardinal ones. Each player solves max u_i(s_i, s_-i): coupled optimization problems, not one LP. (1) See it in motion, standard animation, about 52 s, scenario .seg Menu of outputs: '30, 40' / '30, 40, 60' (default) / '20, 30, 40, 60', every cell computed from P = 1000 - 5(q1 + q2), c = 400, profits in billion COP per month. Chapters: 'From price to table' (the price line folds into a grid, cells fill with staggered entrances); 'Cross out dominated outputs' (one elimination round at a time, both plants together, the compared payoffs pulse: 10 > 9, 8 > 6, 4 > 0; rounds are 1, 2 and 3 for the three menus, because in the 4 output menu 60 ties with 40 against 20 and only falls after 20 is gone); 'Nobody moves alone' (vertical arrows for the row plant, horizontal for the column plant, the cell with no outgoing arrow ringed in accent red: (40, 40) with 8 and 8); 'Every cell is a point' (cells fly into the (pi1, pi2) plane, Pareto frontier in ink); 'Stable, not optimal' (final frame: faded table, equilibrium, the Pareto better cell (30, 30) with 9 and 9 in bright red, joint loss 2 of 18). HUD chips: Cells left, Rounds, Equilibrium, Profits, Best joint cell. With menu '30, 40' the HUD reads dominant strategy equilibrium, T 10 > R 9 > P 8 > S 7.5 and 2R > T + S. No best response plane, no staircase, no profit curves (those belong to Price Wars). (2) Your table (workbench). Source .seg: Market (2 to 4 output sliders; hover shows Q, P, margin and both profits) / Classics (prisoner's dilemma 3, 0, 5, 1; Gibbons 2x3 Up, Down against Left, Middle, Right ending at (Up, Middle) with (1, 2); mixture example T (3, 0), M (0, 3), B (1, 1); weak order example rows U (1,1) (0,0), M (1,1) (2,1), D (0,0) (2,1) against L, R, which ends at (2, 1) or (1, 1) depending on the deletion order; driving side; Hi-Lo; battle of the sexes; stag hunt; chicken; matching pennies as the cliffhanger with no pure equilibrium) / Free (any table up to 4x4) / Random (Anim.rng seed). Lens .seg on the same table: Dominance (pair badges strict, weak, none; 'Dominated by a mix?' with the LP weights and margin; with two columns rows are drawn as points and the T to M segment passes above B; Step and Run buttons for elimination with a reason sentence built from the compared numbers; strict or weak toggle; small strip 'Guess p of the average', p from 0.1 to 0.9, bounds 100 p^k and Nagel's first round mean near 37) / Best responses (underline mode: the visitor marks what she thinks are the best responses and the page checks and explains; arrows; pure equilibria ringed; belief slider over two rival columns with three expected payoff lines, their upper envelope and the switch point, 1/3 for the market with rival 30 or 60, and 60 never a best response; Monte Carlo counter of random games with 0, 1 or 2+ pure equilibria) / Payoff space (cells as points, convex hull, Pareto frontier, equilibria, cell of max pi1 + pi2; symmetric 2x2 classifier with T, R, P, S sliders that names the family live: prisoner's dilemma, stag hunt, chicken, harmony, deadlock, and draws dominance arrows; a Market button loads T, R, P, S from two outputs). Cournot as a potential game: chip with argmax of F = (a - c)(q1 + q2) - b(q1^2 + q2^2 + q1 q2) over the table, which is the equilibrium. (3) The price of going alone, scenario .seg Shared lake / Two roads. Lake: n fishers (1 to 30) on a shared ciénaga, catch x_i, earnings x_i(a - X), a = 120 (illustrative): equilibrium a/(n + 1) each, welfare n a^2/(n + 1)^2 against a^2/4, ratio (n + 1)^2/(4n), per unit fee slider and the fee that restores the optimum, a(n - 1)/(2n); note that with n = 2 this is exactly Price Wars divided by 5, where the firms' optimum is a cartel that hurts buyers (efficient for whom). Roads: Pigou, one unit of traffic, road A 1 hour, road B x^d, d from 1 to 8: equilibrium 1, optimum, price of anarchy, marginal cost toll toggle d x^d that makes the selfish split optimal. (4) Under each block an optimization strip (TeX.set with live numbers): each player's problem, the mixture LP, the potential, planner against equilibrium, Beckmann potential against total time. (5) Model card, What to notice (live numbers only), Further reading (Nash 1950; Gibbons 1992; Nagel 1995; Flood and Dresher, Tucker 1950; Axelrod 1984; Schelling 1960; Goldberg, Goldman and Newman 1968; Monderer and Shapley 1996; Hardin 1968; Pigou 1920; Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou 1999; Roughgarden and Tardos 2002), footer note (plants, lake and roads illustrative; Gibbons, Axelrod and Nagel data from the sources). Trims if needed: beauty contest strip, Monte Carlo, toll toggle.
pages.live_computation: In page engine for any m x n bimatrix (m, n up to 4): cells from the Cournot formula; pure best responses and pure Nash equilibria by scanning; pairwise strict and weak dominance with tie detection (menus such as 30, 40, 50, 60 contain ties, 40 and 50 both give 10 against 30, so wording must stay tie aware); dominance by a mixture with LP.solve: max e' s.t. sum_k s_k u(k, j) - e' >= u(s, j) - M for every column j, sum_k s_k = 1, s, e' >= 0, with e = e' - M (M = payoff range + 1), dominated iff e > 1e-9; elimination log round by round (strict: order free; weak: both orders run to show the dependence); belief envelope by intersecting lines; random games with Anim.rng(seed) and a live Monte Carlo (2x2 tends to 1/8, 3/4, 1/8; n x n climbs slowly toward 1/e, about 0.21 at 3x3, 0.30 at 6x6, 0.33 at 10x10, so never claim fast convergence); hull and Pareto frontier by sorting; potential maximized on the grid; commons and Pigou in closed form with a numeric golden section cross check. Anchors verified in Python: 3x3 table (9, 9), (7.5, 10), (4.5, 9), (8, 8), (4, 6), (0, 0) with mirrored cells; elimination 60 then 30 to (40, 40); menu 20, 30, 40, 60: 20 by 30, then 60 by 40, then 30 by 40; mixture margin 0.5 with weights (1/2, 1/2); Gibbons to (Up, Middle) with (1, 2); belief lines 4.5 + 4.5t, 4 + 6t, 9t with switch at 1/3; potential argmax (40, 40); commons 3200 against 3600 for n = 2 (ratio 9/8), 3.025 for n = 10, fee 30 for n = 2; Pigou optimum 0.75 and 0.615, price of anarchy 1.333 and 1.626 at d = 1 and 2.

concepts_covered: NC7 Coordination games: the mixed equilibrium as a tipping share (Hi-Lo 1/3, driving side 1/2)
NC8 Battle of the sexes: two pure and one mixed equilibrium, mix set by the other's payoffs
NC9 Stag hunt: payoff dominance versus risk dominance, basins of attraction
NC10 Chicken and Hawk-Dove: anti-coordination, crash probability, evolutionarily stable share V/C
NC11 Matching pennies and rock paper scissors: no pure equilibrium, predictor game, fictitious play
NC12 Mixed strategies, indifference principle, Nash's existence theorem, penalty kicks with real data
NC13 Zero sum games: security levels, maximin, minimax, saddle points, 2 x n graphical method
NC14 Minimax theorem as LP strong duality (Odd or Even, rock paper scissors)
NC21 Correlated equilibrium as an LP (optional box, the traffic light)
pages.pitch_es: Juegas 30 rondas de cara o sello contra una máquina que aprende tus patrones y compruebas que lo único seguro es lanzar la moneda al 50 %. Después ves en un cuadrado cómo se cruzan las mejores respuestas de dos jugadores que mezclan, por qué la mezcla de cada uno la deciden los pagos del otro, y lo confirmas con los datos reales de penales de Palacios-Huerta (2003). Al final resuelves cualquier juego de suma cero con un PL cuyo dual es el PL del rival, y en pares o nones descubres que quien pide nones gana 1/12 por jugada aunque el juego parezca justo.
pages.sections: File site/lab/be-unpredictable.html, bundle lab/lab-gtb-mix (prefix gtm), eyebrow 'Lab · Proposal · Game'. (1) Beat the machine (game, first on the page): 30 rounds of Heads or Tails against a predictor that reads the visitor's last one or two moves (in the spirit of Shannon's mind reading machine); the machine wins on a match; live win rate with the fair coin band; button 'Let a coin play for me'; toggle rock paper scissors (equilibrium 1/3 each, value 0). Wording: the machine punishes predictable patterns, only the 1/2, 1/2 mix guarantees the value against every opponent, 30 rounds prove nothing. Below, a small fictitious play panel (Brown 1951, Robinson 1951): each side best responds to the other's empirical frequencies, the point spirals in to (1/2, 1/2) and the guaranteed band closes. (2) See it in motion, standard animation, about 50 s, scenario .seg Battle of the sexes / Stag hunt / Chicken / Matching pennies. Chapters: 'Four cells, four corners' (the 2x2 table folds into the unit square of mixes (p, q), deviation arrows along the edges); 'Two payoff lines' (each player's expected payoffs against the rival's mix and their crossing, the indifference point); 'Best response paths' (the Z shaped correspondences, accent red for the row player, ink for the column player); 'Where paths cross' (3 equilibria, or 1 for pennies); 'What mixing costs' (final frame with payoffs: battle of the sexes p = 2/3, q = 1/3, 2/3 each, below the worst pure payoff 1, mismatch 5/9; stag hunt stag with 3/4, payoff 3, deviation loss products 1 against 9 so Hare is risk dominant; chicken swerve 9/10, payoff -0.1, crash 1/100; pennies 1/2 and value 0). HUD: p*, q*, Payoffs, Equilibria, Mismatch or crash. (3) Solve any 2x2 (simulation on the same square): payoff sliders and presets (the four classics, Hi-Lo, driving side, Hawk-Dove with V and C sliders, penalty kicks with Palacios-Huerta's scoring rates N/N 58.30, N/O 94.97, O/N 92.91, O/O 69.92); live pure and mixed equilibria, indifference formulas typeset with the current numbers, the count of equilibria (odd, Wilson 1971; Nash 1950 guarantees at least one), the demo 'your mix is set by your rival': dragging player 1's Opera value moves only q*; crash cost slider K for chicken (swerve 1 - 1/K). For symmetric games a population strip on [0, 1] with replicator flow arrows and trajectories from a starting share: the mixed equilibrium is a watershed in coordination games (Hi-Lo 1/3, driving 1/2, stag hunt 3/4) and an attractor in Hawk-Dove (V/C, 1/2 with V = 2, C = 4; Hawk dominant when V >= C). Penalty readout: kicker natural side 38.5 %, keeper natural side 42.0 %, scoring 79.6 %, observed about 40 % and 42 %; a keeper who always dives to the natural side concedes 94.97 %. Optional 20 x 20 town of agents best responding to neighbours (Anim.rng). (4) Zero sum: guarantee and LP (simulation): matrix up to 5x5, presets saddle 3x3 [[4, 4, 10], [2, 3, 1], [6, 5, 7]] (value 5 at row 3, column 2), no saddle [[4, 1], [2, 3]] (maximin 2 < 2.5 < minimax 3), Odd or Even [[-2, 3], [3, -4]] ('pares o nones'), rock paper scissors, penalty 2x2; row minima, column maxima, maximin, minimax and saddle marker; for 2 x n the graphical method with draggable p and the shaded lower envelope; the row player's LP and the column player's LP side by side with equal optimal values (minimax theorem = strong duality), the column mix read from the duals, a complementary slackness table (strategy used, constraint binding: the indifference principle); Simulate 1,000 / 10,000 / 100,000 rounds with the running average and its 95 % band. (5) Optional closed box 'The traffic light': Aumann's chicken (6, 6), (2, 7), (7, 2), (0, 0); LP over correlated equilibria maximizing total payoff, four incentive rows with slack and dual: (1/2, 1/4, 1/4, 0) with 5.25 each, against 14/3 = 4.67 for mixed Nash and 5 for the uniform device; editable 2x2 or 3x3. (6) Optimization strips, model card (simplex of mixes, x^T A y, indifference conditions, primal and dual minimax LPs in the aligned format, CE LP), What to notice, Further reading (von Neumann 1928; Nash 1950, 1951; Brown 1951; Robinson 1951; Dantzig 1951; Luce and Raiffa 1957; Lemke and Howson 1964; Wilson 1971; Maynard Smith and Price 1973; Aumann 1974; Harsanyi and Selten 1988; Palacios-Huerta 2003), footer note (predictor, town and Hawk-Dove values illustrative; penalty rates from Palacios-Huerta). Trims if needed: town grid, CE box, rock paper scissors in the game.
pages.live_computation: Predictor with order 1 and order 2 transition counts of the visitor's moves, fallback to overall frequencies, ties by Anim.rng(seed); win rate with band 0.5 +/- 1.96 sqrt(0.25/n) (about +/- 0.18 at 30 rounds). Fictitious play (simultaneous, ties to the first strategy) storing empirical mixes and the band [min_j (x_bar A)_j, max_i (A y_bar)_i]. 2x2 solver: pure equilibria by scanning, mixed equilibrium by indifference (valid when strictly inside (0, 1)), best response correspondences, expected payoffs, mismatch and crash probabilities, replicator flow dx/dt = x(1 - x)(Delta u(x)) for symmetric games. Zero sum: row minima, column maxima, saddle detection; lower envelope for 2 x n by line intersections; LP.solve on A + k with k = 1 - min a_ij (max v s.t. sum_i x_i (a_ij + k) - v >= 0 for every column j, sum_i x_i = 1, x, v >= 0), y* from the duals of the column rows, value minus k, cross checked against the column LP within 1e-6; simulation with Anim.rng and band 1.96 sigma / sqrt(n) computed from the equilibrium distribution (for Odd or Even sigma is about 2.92, so the band is about +/- 0.18 after 1,000 rounds, +/- 0.057 after 10,000 and +/- 0.018 after 100,000: the 1/12 edge only shows clearly with the large runs, never claim it at 1,000). CE LP with LP.solve (4 or 9 variables, incentive rows, sum = 1). Anchors verified in Python: battle of the sexes (2/3, 1/3), 2/3 each, mismatch 5/9; stag hunt 3/4, payoff 3, products 1 and 9; chicken 9/10, -0.1, crash 1/100; Hi-Lo 1/3, 2/3 each; Hawk-Dove 1/2; penalty 38.54 %, 41.99 %, 79.57 %; 3x3 saddle value 5; [[4, 1], [2, 3]] x = (1/4, 3/4), y = (1/2, 1/2), value 2.5; Odd or Even (7/12, 5/12) for both, value 1/12, shifted by 5 gives 61/12; CE (1/2, 1/4, 1/4, 0) with 5.25 each.

pages.title_es: Teoría de juegos 3: Jugada a jugada
concepts_covered: NC15 Extensive form, strategies as contingent plans, backward induction, subgame perfect equilibrium, non credible threats (entry deterrence; Stackelberg as the subgame perfect equilibrium of the discrete Price Wars tree)
NC16 Ultimatum game: subgame perfection versus Nash outcomes and observed behaviour
NC17 Centipede game: the paradox of backward induction, simplified reputation threshold
NC18 Repeated games: finite horizon unravelling, grim trigger and tit for tat thresholds, Axelrod tournaments, folk theorem
NC19 Pareto versus equilibrium revisited (centipede, repeated dilemma)
pages.pitch_es: Muchas decisiones se toman por turnos, y un árbol de jugadas se resuelve desde las hojas hacia la raíz, como un problema de programación dinámica. La animación lo hace con una planta que piensa entrar a competir, con el líder de Guerra de precios (que vuelve a producir 60 kt contra 30 del seguidor, ahora en un árbol) y con el ciempiés, donde una lógica impecable deja a los dos jugadores con la dieciseisava parte de lo que podían ganar. Abajo editas los pagos, ves qué amenazas no son creíbles, juegas el ultimátum contra una población de respondedores y pones a competir ojo por ojo, gatillo y otras estrategias en un dilema repetido con la probabilidad de seguir jugando que tú escojas.
pages.sections: File site/lab/move-by-move.html, bundle lab/lab-gtb-moves (prefix gts), eyebrow 'Lab · Proposal · Animation'. Keep the tree vocabulary consistent with the Roll Back the Tree resource (decision trees), but here every node belongs to a player. (1) See it in motion, standard animation, about 54 s, scenario .seg Entry / Leader and follower / Centipede. Chapters: 'A tree of moves' (the tree grows from the root with staggered branches, leaf payoffs appear; a dashed information set shows how a simultaneous move would look); 'Start at the leaves' (last movers choose, winning branch in accent red, losing branch silver, values climb as chips); 'Roll back to the root' (the subgame perfect path glows); chapter 4 is scenario specific: 'Threats that bluff' for Entry and Leader (the induced normal form slides in beside the tree, all its pure Nash equilibria are marked and the ones resting on a non credible threat flash bright red: (Out, Fight) in Entry; in Leader the follower's plan 'always 40' that would push the leader back to Cournot (40, 40) with 8 and 8) and 'Logic against gain' for Centipede (the end payoff, 16 times larger for both, next to the take at once outcome); 'Plan versus outcome' (final frame: subgame perfect path and payoffs beside the Nash outcomes it rules out). Classic data: entry deterrence after Selten (Out gives (0, 2); In, then Accommodate (1, 1) or Fight (-1, -1)); leader and follower with outputs 30, 40, 60 and profits from the Price Wars formula (leader 60, follower 30, profits 9 and 4.5 against 8 and 8; the follower's threat to stay at 40 is not credible because 4.0 < 4.5); McKelvey and Palfrey four move centipede (take payoffs (0.40, 0.10), (0.20, 0.80), (1.60, 0.40), (0.80, 3.20), end (6.40, 1.60)). HUD chips: Nodes solved, Subgame perfect outcome, Payoffs, Nash equilibria, Not credible. (2) Edit the tree (simulation on the same engine): editable leaves for the three trees; slider for the incumbent's payoff from fighting (for example after investing in capacity) with the live threshold (above 1 entry is deterred); leader and follower output menu from the Price Wars formula, shown as a bilevel problem (the leader optimizes subject to the follower's optimal reply); centipede with 2 to 10 nodes and a growth factor, the gap between the subgame perfect payoff and the end payoff, a reputation slider a (share of partners who always pass) with the live threshold (1/31 = 3.2 % for the base data; simplification declared on the page, Kreps, Milgrom, Roberts and Wilson 1982). (3) Ultimatum (game): split 10 coins; responder populations 'rational' and 'fair minded' (illustrative presets) or a custom histogram of minimum acceptable offers; acceptance A(x), expected payoff (10 - x) A(x) as bars with its maximizer; the visitor makes offers to responders drawn with Anim.rng and compares realized and expected; the tree shows the two subgame perfect equilibria with integer offers (offer 1, or 0 if indifferent responders accept) and why every split is a Nash outcome under the threat 'accept only if x >= x*'; experimental facts as text (mean offers 30 to 40 %, mode often 50 %, offers below 20 % rejected about half the time; Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze 1982; Camerer 2003). (4) Play it again (simulation): repeated prisoner's dilemma with T, R, P, S sliders (default 5, 3, 1, 0); a discount axis with the grim threshold (T - R)/(T - P) and the tit for tat threshold max((T - R)/(T - P), (T - R)/(R - S)); a 'known last round' toggle that unravels cooperation by backward induction over the rounds; round robin among always cooperate, always defect, tit for tat, grim, tit for two tats, win stay lose shift and random, with continuation probability w (expected length 1/(1 - w)), noise e and a seed; score table and an ecological run where shares grow with score; folk theorem picture with the feasible payoffs, the minmax point (1, 1) and the sustainable set as d grows. Axelrod's tournaments as text (first: 14 entries plus RANDOM, 200 moves per match; second: 62 plus RANDOM; tit for tat won both without ever beating its opponent in a match). (5) Optimization strips (Bellman recursion of backward induction, the leader's bilevel problem, the two geometric series of the trigger condition, the best reply to tit for tat as a small MDP), model card, What to notice, Further reading (Zermelo 1913; Kuhn 1953; Selten 1965, 1978; Bellman 1957; Rosenthal 1981; Kreps, Milgrom, Roberts and Wilson 1982; McKelvey and Palfrey 1992; Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze 1982; Camerer 2003; Friedman 1971; Axelrod 1980, 1984; Fudenberg and Maskin 1986), footer note (entrant and incumbent payoffs, responder populations and tournament settings illustrative; centipede and Axelrod data from the sources). Trims if needed: folk theorem picture, ecological run, tit for two tats and win stay lose shift.
pages.live_computation: Tree engine: nodes with a player and children, leaves with payoff vectors; backward induction by post order recursion with a declared tie rule, listing both subgame perfect equilibria when a tie matters (ultimatum zero offer); induced normal form by enumerating every player's contingent plans (entry 2 x 2; leader and follower 3 x 27 = 81 cells; centipede reduced 3 x 3), pure Nash equilibria by scanning, each flagged subgame perfect or not by comparing with the backward induction plan; leader and follower profits from the same Cournot formula as page 1. Ultimatum: A(x) from the chosen distribution, (10 - x) A(x) and its argmax. Centipede: piles grow by the factor, backward induction, gap, reputation threshold from (1 - a) times the payoff of being taken from at node 2 plus a times the end payoff against taking at node 1. Repeated dilemma: thresholds in closed form; tournament matches with geometric length (continuation w) and noise e drawn with Anim.rng(seed), mean payoff per move per pair; ecological update x_k <- x_k score_k / mean score. Anchors verified in Python: entry has 2 pure Nash equilibria, subgame perfect (In, Accommodate) with (1, 1), deterrence when the fight payoff exceeds 1; leader and follower have 12 pure Nash equilibria (outcome (60, 30) six times, (40, 40) four, (30, 40) two) and one subgame perfect equilibrium: leader 60, follower plan 30 to 40, 40 to 40, 60 to 30, profits 9 and 4.5, equal to the continuous Stackelberg of Price Wars; centipede: take at once (0.40, 0.10) against the end (6.40, 1.60), the reduced normal form has a single Nash equilibrium with that same outcome (so no 'non credible threat' chapter there), threshold a* = 1/31 = 3.2 %; ultimatum with rational responders: offer 1 (or 0); thresholds 1/2 (grim) and 2/3 (tit for tat) for 5, 3, 1, 0.

pages.title_es: Teoría de juegos 4: Reparte el ahorro
concepts_covered: C1 Cooperation with side payments: TU games (N, v), bridge from Price Wars (binding agreement worth 12.5 % more profit, legal alliances only)
C2 Characteristic function computed by optimization (Giapetto LP per coalition)
C3 Cost games, savings games, subadditivity and superadditivity
C4 Imputations: efficiency and individual rationality, the barycentric triangle
C5 The core: stand alone and incremental cost tests, no cross subsidy
C6 Core LP, least core, cost of stability
C7 Balanced collections and the Bondareva-Shapley theorem (duals as weights)
C8 LP games: Owen's shadow price allocation; assignment game core as optimal duals (closed box)
C9 Convex (supermodular) games and concave cost games
C10 Marginal vectors and the Weber set
C11 Shapley value: axioms, subset formula, average of arrival orders, Harsanyi dividends
C12 Glove game: core versus Shapley outside it
C13 Airport game (segment rule)
C14 Least core to nucleolus by a sequence of LPs
C15 Bankruptcy and the Talmud (nucleolus), proportional, CEA, CEL
C16 Practical rules: equal split, proportional, SCRB, core check
C17 Minimum cost spanning tree games and Bird's rule
C18 Inventory centralization: EOQ joint ordering and the SOC rule
C19 Spare parts pooling with Erlang loss (bridge to the study section)
C20 Stability versus fairness and monotonicity (rules by properties matrix)
pages.pitch_es: Tres empresas comparten un centro de distribución y ahorran 35 millones de pesos al mes: ¿cómo se reparten la cuenta sin que ninguna empresa ni ninguna pareja prefiera irse por su lado? Cada coalición tiene su propio costo óptimo, el núcleo es un polígono de repartos estables dentro de un triángulo y un PL te dice si existe; cuando no existe, su dual te da el certificado y el subsidio que salvaría la alianza. Las empresas llegan en distinto orden y el promedio de sus costos marginales es el valor de Shapley, mientras una sucesión de PL encoge las quejas hasta el nucléolo, y con un deslizador ves cuándo los dos son estables y cuándo Shapley se sale. Al final comparas reglas (partes iguales, proporcional, SCRB, Shapley, nucléolo) en juegos clásicos: guantes, aeropuerto, el problema del Talmud, una red compartida y un fondo común de repuestos.
pages.sections: File site/lab/share-the-savings.html, bundle lab/lab-gtb-share (prefix gtc), eyebrow 'Lab · Proposal · Simulation'. Running example (illustrative, million COP per month): firms A, B, C share a distribution center; alone 40, 50, 60; pairs AB 65, AC 85, BC 95; all three 115; saving 35. The pair cost c(AB) is the lever that walks through every regime: 70 to 90 concave cost (convex savings, Weber set = core), 62.5 to 70 Shapley still in the core, 55 to 62.5 Shapley outside, below 55 the core is empty (at exactly 55 it is a segment); presets avoid the exact borders 55, 62.5 and 70. (0) Lede and a 'Contracts change the game' box that picks up page 1's Pareto gap: binding agreements and side payments (TU); in Price Wars a binding agreement would raise total profit by 12.5 % (18 against 16 billion COP), but price collusion is illegal, so cooperative models serve legal alliances (shared warehouses, joint transport, spare parts pools); cost game c and savings game v(S) = sum c(i) - c(S) give the same allocations. (1) See it in motion, standard animation, about 56 s, scenario .seg Weak pair (c(AB) = 80) / Middle (65) / Strong pair (60). Chapters: 'Seven bills' (stand alone bars merge into pooled bars for each coalition, saving 35 as a bright red chip); 'Splits nobody rejects' (imputation triangle whose corners give the whole saving to one firm, six coalition lines sweep in with forbidden sides shaded, the core polygon remains: hexagon at 80, quadrilateral at 65 and 60); 'Firms arrive in turn' (six arrival orders as quick sequences, each drops its marginal vector, Weber hexagon, in or out badges: 6 in at 80, 2 in at 65 and 60); 'The average order' (Shapley = mean of the six, inside at 80 and 65, outside at 60 where A and B pay 61.67 > 60); 'Shrink the complaints' (epsilon core shrinking with the LP rounds: one round at 80 and 65, two at 60); 'Stable or fair' (final frame: core, Weber set, Shapley, nucleolus and chips). HUD chips: Saving, Core, Shapley, Nucleolus, LP rounds. (2) Your alliance (workbench). (3) Optimization strips, model card (coalition LP v(S), imputation set, core polytope, core LP and its dual (balancedness), least core LP, Owen theorem by weak duality, Shapley formula, nucleolus LP of round k, Erlang B recursion), What to notice, Further reading (von Neumann and Morgenstern 1944; Gillies 1959; Bondareva 1963; Shapley 1953, 1967, 1971; Schmeidler 1969; Kopelowitz 1967; Maschler, Peleg and Shapley 1979; Owen 1975; Shapley and Shubik 1971; Littlechild and Owen 1973; Faulhaber 1975; Bird 1976; Granot and Huberman 1981; Aumann and Maschler 1985; Young 1985; Weber 1988; Sprumont 1990; Meca, Timmer, García-Jurado and Borm 2004; Bachrach et al. 2009; Karsten, Slikker and van Houtum 2012), footer note (all costs, ownerships, network and pooling parameters illustrative; Talmud claims and glove, airport and majority games are the textbook cases). pages.live_computation: One in page engine for any TU game with n up to 5 (31 coalitions; the triangle only when n = 3): cost and savings forms; subadditivity, superadditivity and supermodularity checks that name the failing inequality; core polygon by clipping the imputation triangle with the six half planes, with its vertex list; core LP with LP.solve (min sum x_i s.t. x(S) >= v(S) for proper S, zero normalized savings so x >= 0), duals = balancing weights lambda_S (certificate sum lambda_S v(S) against v(N), cost of stability z* - v(N)); least core with epsilon = e+ - e-; nucleolus by the LP sequence (Kopelowitz; Maschler, Peleg and Shapley) with x_i >= v(i) kept as rows, one extra LP per tight coalition to decide which are fixed (a positive dual proves fixed, a zero dual does not prove free), tolerance 1e-7 relative; Shapley by the subset formula and by the n! orders as a cross check, dividends; marginal vectors and Weber hull; rules: equal, proportional, driver, SCRB with SC_i = c(N) - c(N minus i), Owen from the grand coalition duals, Bird from the MST, SOC = c(i)^2 / c(N), Talmud by CEA and CEL on half claims cross checked against the nucleolus; property scores by re-solving. Generators: Giapetto LP per coalition (7 LP.solve; demand cap must be below 20 soldiers to bind, since the optimum uses 20: with 25 the grand optimum and duals stay (1, 1, 0), with exactly 20 the dual is degenerate, with 10 the duals become (0, 2, 1) and Owen (45, 82.5, 42.5)), Kruskal per coalition, EOQ square root law, Erlang B recursion B(k) = aB(k - 1)/(k + aB(k - 1)) with integer search of the base stock, bankruptcy max(0, E - sum of outside claims), airport max, glove min(L, R), majority a. rationale_es:
Te propongo un recorrido de cuatro páginas en el orden de un curso clásico: 1) juegos simultáneos en estrategias puras, 2) mezclas y suma cero, 3) juegos por turnos y repetidos, 4) juegos cooperativos. La 2 y la 3 solo necesitan la 1, y la 4 necesita la brecha de Pareto de la 1 y la dualidad de PL (de la 2 o del recurso de precios sombra). Cada página gira alrededor de un solo objeto que el visitante manipula, para que no quede como una lista de widgets sueltos: la 1 es una tabla de pagos que se mira con tres lentes (dominancia, mejores respuestas, espacio de pagos); la 2 es el cuadrado unitario de las mezclas más el PL de un juego de suma cero; la 3 es un motor de árboles que se resuelve desde las hojas; la 4 es el triángulo de imputaciones de un juego de tres jugadores, con un solo motor que calcula núcleo, Shapley y nucléolo para ocho conjuntos de datos. Todas tienen la misma forma: una animación estándar de 50 a 56 segundos con su ejemplo clásico, un bloque práctico que recalcula todo en vivo y, bajo cada bloque, una franja de optimización con la fórmula viva: PL de dominancia por mezcla, eliminación como presolve y potencial de Cournot (1); PL minimax y su dual, holgura complementaria como principio de indiferencia y PL del equilibrio correlacionado (2); programación dinámica, problema binivel del líder y comparación de series geométricas (3); un PL por coalición, PL del núcleo con su dual de Bondareva y Shapley, reparto de Owen con precios sombra, Shapley como promedio de vectores marginales y nucléolo como sucesión de PL (4).

Guerra de precios no se repite: sus datos (P = 1000 - 5Q, c = 400) se discretizan en una tabla de 30, 40 y 60 kt, donde aparece un dilema del prisionero escondido en el mercado del cemento (1), y en un árbol de líder y seguidor que reproduce el Stackelberg de 60 y 30 kt sin el plano ni la escalera (3). Frente a la lista corta anterior: la página 4 reemplaza a "Un reparto que ningún grupo rechaza" (no construyas ambas; sus casos de lechería y camión pueden volver como conjuntos de datos); la 2 usa pares o nones, piedra, papel o tijera y el penal 2x2 de Palacios-Huerta, y deja a "Minimax en el punto penal" el 3x3 con centro, el aprendizaje y la tanda; la 1 mide el precio de la anarquía con Pigou y los comunes y deja Braess a "El atajo que nos atrasa a todos" (si esa no se construye, Braess entra como tercer escenario de la 1); "Los guardaparques juegan primero" complementa la 3 (compromiso con una estrategia mixta). La 4 cierra con un fondo común de repuestos (Karsten, Slikker y van Houtum, 2012) como puerta hacia la sección de estudio sobre la investigación de Loe Schlicher, sin adelantar su contenido.

Recalculé en Python con scipy los números de anclaje de las cuatro páginas y encontré matices que el constructor debe respetar. En Giapetto el tope de demanda de soldados debe ser menor que 20 para pesar: con 25 el óptimo sigue en 20 soldados y los duales no cambian, con 20 el dual es degenerado y con 10 los duales pasan a 0, 2 y 1. En el centro de distribución, con c(AB) = 55 el núcleo todavía existe (es un segmento) y solo queda vacío por debajo; 62,5 y 70 son fronteras exactas, así que los presets las evitan. El juego discreto de líder y seguidor tiene 12 equilibrios de Nash puros y uno solo perfecto en subjuegos, mientras el ciempiés reducido tiene un único Nash con el mismo resultado; por eso el capítulo 4 de la página 3 cambia de nombre según el escenario. En juegos aleatorios n x n la fracción sin equilibrio puro sube despacio hacia 1/e (0,21 en 3x3, 0,30 en 6x6, 0,33 en 10x10). Algunos menús de Cournot traen empates (con 30, 40, 50 y 60, contra 30 da igual producir 40 o 50) y el editor debe detectarlos. En pares o nones la ventaja de 1/12 queda tapada por el ruido en 1.000 rondas (banda de más o menos 0,18) y solo se ve con 100.000. Los comunes con a = 120 son Guerra de precios dividida por 5 (3.200 contra 3.600, o sea 16 contra 18 mil millones de pesos), pero allí el óptimo de las firmas es un cartel que perjudica a los compradores. El juego de repuestos no es convexo y dos de sus vectores marginales quedan fuera del núcleo, aunque proporcional, Shapley y nucléolo quedan dentro; la página lo comprueba en vivo y no lo presenta como teorema. Esfuerzo: tres páginas L y una M (la 3). Te sugiero construir primero la 1, cuyo motor de tablas reutilizan la 2 y la 3, y que el líder agregue un módulo compartido pequeño (por ejemplo site/assets/games.js) para no copiar ese motor en tres páginas. Los scripts de verificación quedaron en /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-repo/c29c830a-c0ee-54bb-9a58-8c9f26c80fec/scratchpad/gtbasics/.
